text: AI agents are starting to spend money and hire people. When an agent overspends, or the work never happens, who is accountable?
SettleAI is the accountability layer. A person signs what an agent may do. The money waits, proof is checked, and every decision leaves a receipt anyone can verify.
Ravi has signed a mandate for his agent: delivery jobs only, up to one hundred fifty dollars each, four hundred in total.
The agent tries a five hundred dollar job outside that mandate. Mandate Guard is deterministic code. It denies the request before any money moves, and says why.
Inside the mandate, the agent hires a courier. Ravi funds the job on the PayPal sandbox, with Orders version two. The money is held on the platform account until the work is proven.
The worker submits a photo. Rules check location, time and duplicates first. Then a vision model judges each criterion, and policy approves the release.

Ravi disputes the delivery and adds a photo of the damage. The arbiter returns a liability finding that cites the mandate clause, the criteria and the evidence. Both sides accept, and PayPal settles it.
Someone reuses that photo on another job. The perceptual hash catches it, the payout is held, and it waits in the risk queue for a person.
Every step is signed into a receipt. Anyone can verify it, without trusting us. Change one byte, and verification fails, pointing to the broken link.
In our repeatable test scenarios, no bad proof was auto-paid, and every tampered receipt was caught. Next: production key custody, a regulated partner, and PayPal Invoicing.
This runs on the PayPal sandbox with test money. The mandates are inspired by AP2. They are not official, and not endorsed by PayPal.
